Stanford · Koyejo Group · judge-free evaluation · v2, revised after Brando's review

Grading models against a gold reference
measures skill on hard tasks, style on easy ones

Can you score models without an LLM judge, by checking their work against a benchmark's gold solutions? We tested the sharpest version of that idea: TFA, which scores a model by how well it predicts the reference solution token by token. Seventeen models, seven families, eight math and code benchmarks. On hard problems it gives you a real leaderboard: models that predict the reference well are the models that solve problems well. On easy, saturated benchmarks that connection goes away, because everyone predicts the reference about equally well and the leftover differences are writing style, not skill; on GSM8K the ranking actually flips.

17 models · 7 families · 8 datasets (math · olympiad · code) · every headline correlation reported as Pearson r / r² + Spearman ρ + Kendall τ
scroll or press → to advance
The takeaway

Three results, stated up front

+0.86 / +0.84 / +0.71hard math: ρ / r / τ, TFA vs accuracy
−0.25 / −0.14 / −0.16saturated GSM8K: ρ / r / τ
≈ 0grading one solution, all variants

1 · TFA can rank models, if the benchmark is hard

We compared mean TFA to accuracy for 17 models from 7 families. On Putnam and olympiad math the two agree closely. The agreement fades as benchmarks get easier, and on GSM8K it goes negative: the models with the best TFA are not the most accurate ones. Same story on SWE-bench: TFA ranks the four Qwen-Coder sizes correctly, and tells you nothing when comparing across families.

2 · TFA cannot grade a single solution

We checked whether a solution's TFA tracks the grade a judge gives that solution. It does not: 89-96% of what per-solution TFA measures is how predictable the reference text is, which says nothing about the solution being graded. We tried seven fixes and none recovered a signal. Earlier work assumed TFA could stand in for a judge here; as far as we can tell, nobody had actually tested it.

3 · Grading without a judge is possible, just expensive

One thing did grade: cut a solution off partway, have a fixed model finish it, and check whether it still lands on the right answer. That correlates +0.43 with the judge's grade and even tells sound solutions from lucky ones. The catch: it needs many completions per solution, roughly 100x the compute of TFA.

The reason behind all three. On a hard problem, predicting the reference's next step takes the same skill as solving the problem. On an easy problem everyone can predict it, so whatever differences remain come from formatting and phrasing. When the benchmark is easy, that is all TFA has left to measure.

Terms used in this deck

Five terms, defined before we use them

TFA (Teacher-Forced Accuracy). Give the model the problem, then feed it the gold solution one token at a time. At each position, ask: would the model have predicted this next token itself? TFA is the fraction of positions where the answer is yes. It takes one deterministic forward pass, and no judge or rubric is involved anywhere.
Model-level correlation. Answers: can TFA build a leaderboard? Each model gets one number, its average TFA over all problems, and we correlate that with its accuracy across the 17 models. If the most accurate model also has the highest average TFA, the second most accurate the second highest, and so on, Spearman ρ comes out +1.
Item-level correlation. Answers: can TFA grade one answer? Take a single solution and ask whether its TFA tracks the grade a judge gives it, after right-vs-wrong is factored out (a partial correlation controlling for correctness). Concretely: the judge gives one solution 0.8 and another 0.3; a grader worth using should score the first clearly higher, even when both end on the correct answer. That is the bar TFA has to clear.
Saturated benchmark. One where every reasonable model scores near the ceiling; on GSM8K, every strong model is above 95%. With that little room for skill to differ, whatever still differs between models is mostly style.
The boundary (map). Our shorthand for the table and figure that record, dataset by dataset, where model-level TFA works and where it fails: clearly positive on hard math, weaker on code, negative on saturated data. When we say SWE-bench "lands on the map", we mean coding agents show the same pattern the map predicts.

One reporting rule for the whole deck: every headline correlation appears three ways, Pearson r (with r²), Spearman ρ (rank order), and Kendall τ (pairwise orderings). Where a figure caption shows only one, the other two are in the table on the boundary-map slide.

Result 1 · ranking · within a family

Start inside one family: TFA tracks accuracy across the Qwen ladder

+0.80 to +0.97Pearson r, within-Qwen, 8 datasets
+0.60 to +1.00Spearman ρ
+0.40 to +1.00Kendall τ

We start with the cleanest comparison we have: five Qwen models, 0.5B to 14B, each reduced to one average-TFA number and one accuracy number per dataset. The left panel plots the correlation between the two under all three statistics. It is positive on all eight datasets, and the weakest values sit on the datasets where accuracy is closest to the ceiling. The right side repeats this same comparison for every other family too. Each family on each dataset gives one correlation number (for example, the three Phi models on GSM8K give one), 29 numbers in all, shown as three histograms split by benchmark type. On hard benchmarks all 13 are positive: every family ranks correctly. On saturated benchmarks 5 of 12 are negative: in those families the stronger models score lower TFA. On code it is 2 of 4.

Inside one family TFA orders models correctly. The histogram also shows where that stops: as soon as the benchmark gets easy.
Result 1 · ranking · across families

Across families it holds on hard math and scrambles on saturated data

Now add Mistral, Phi, OLMo, and the math-specialized families. Each arrow below is one family's size ladder, tail at its smallest model, head at its largest. On hard data (Putnam, MATH-500) the arrows point up-right: a bigger, better model predicts the gold better, whatever family it comes from. As the data gets easier the arrows flatten and scatter, and on GSM8K Phi's and OLMo's arrows point down: their stronger models solve more problems but answer in a fuller, more labeled style than the terse gold, so they predict it worse.

On saturated data a family's house style moves TFA more than its skill does. That is the whole failure mode.

Result 2 · grading · the test

Can TFA grade one solution? No.

≈ 0MATH-500 (item-level partial ρ)
+0.12GSM8K
+0.22Putnam
Reminder of the definition. Item-level means: for one single solution, does TFA track the judge's grade for that solution once right-vs-wrong is removed (partial correlation controlling for correctness)? This is the property you would need to replace a judge with TFA. The statistic here is partial Spearman ρ; the target must be a graded score (a judge, or human grades), because among correct answers plain accuracy has no variance left to correlate with.

The answer is no. The signal is zero on MATH, small on GSM8K, and +0.22 at best on the hardest math. The small values are real (they survive label-noise and contamination controls, and replicate under a second judge from a different model family, appendix), but under 5% of variance is far too little to grade with.

TFA is a leaderboard signal, not a grader. The next slide shows why, with a number.
Result 2 · grading · the reason

89-96% of per-item TFA is about the reference, not the solution

89-96%of per-item variance: reference nuisance
4-11%left over for solution quality

Decompose per-item TFA across the model x item grid: after removing each model's overall level, 89-96% of the remaining variation is identical for every model. It is a fact about the reference (how predictable this particular gold text is), not about the solution being graded. Because it is identical across models it cancels when you average over items, which is why ranking works, and it buries the 4-11% that is actually about quality, which is why grading fails. The full recipe with a worked toy example is in the appendix.

The same number predicts that no reweighting of TFA can fix grading. We tested that prediction seven ways.
Result 2 · grading · seven repairs, all fail

If the signal were merely buried, one of these would have found it

Each repair removes one component of the nuisance: content-token TFA (mask formatting), IDF weighting (up-weight rare tokens), surprisal weighting (up-weight non-formulaic tokens), soft log-prob instead of hard match, step-shuffle contrast (gold minus reordered gold), answer-swap contrast (gold minus wrong-answer gold), multi-reference max (best TFA over several golds). All seven land at zero, and the reweightings go slightly negative: the surprising tokens are exactly the ones good models also miss.

One cautionary tale we keep on purpose. The answer-swap contrast first looked like a +0.35 win. It was a length artifact (the corruption touched only the final token, so the contrast collapsed to "right answer, divided by length"). Controlling for length dropped it to zero, and we retracted it. House rule since: no item-level win is believed until it survives length and difficulty controls.

Seven misses plus the 89-96% decomposition: per-item TFA has no quality signal to recover.
Result 3 · a signal that does grade

Rollout process value grades solutions, at ~100x the cost

+0.43rollout value vs judge grade (ρ)
+0.19separates sound from lucky corrects
~100xcost multiple vs TFA

Drop the reference entirely and measure the solution's own trajectory: truncate it partway, let a fixed completer model finish it, and score whether the completion still reaches the right answer. Averaged over truncation points this "process value" correlates +0.43 with the judge's grade at item level, exactly where TFA sits at zero, and it even separates solutions that are correct for sound reasons from solutions that are correct by luck (+0.19 among corrects only). The catch is compute: many completions per solution instead of one forward pass, roughly a hundredfold.

Grading is possible without a judge, just not cheaply yet. Making this cheap is a real open problem.
Conclusions

What we showed, what is new

The one-sentence version

TFA measures agreement with the reference's style; only on hard data does style move with skill. Everything in this deck is that sentence quantified. And though TFA is the metric we tested, the mechanism belongs to the whole class: any reference-matching metric inherits it.

  • Leaderboards: trustworthy within a family and on hard references (ρ, r, τ all positive); untrustworthy on saturated benchmarks (all three negative on GSM8K).
  • Grading single solutions: fails; 89-96% of the per-item signal belongs to the reference; seven repairs all land at zero.
  • Rollout process value does grade, at ~100x cost.
  • Agents: the identical within-family / cross-family split on SWE-bench patches.

Contributions

  1. First direct test of TFA's item-level grading claim; it fails, and prior work had assumed it.
  2. The mechanism: the 89-96% reference-nuisance decomposition that explains both verdicts at once.
  3. The boundary map in triplicate statistics across 17 models, 7 families, 8 datasets, plus agents.
  4. A grading signal that works (rollout process value) with its cost curve.
Path forward

Our lane: reliable metrics with gold references

Benchmarks and leaderboards already own gold answers; what they lack is a trustworthy way to use them without hiring an LLM judge for every submission. That is the problem this line of work attacks: cheap, deterministic, auditable scoring where a gold reference exists. It is deliberately not the harder problem of evaluation with no gold references (debate, and TVD-MI-style mechanism design). We think the with-references problem is worth solving on its own: it is more tractable precisely because the answer is known, and it is load-bearing because the field's leaderboards run on it.

Design stances

  • Trained metrics are allowed. A metric trained offline and then frozen is much harder to game than a reward model optimized against during RL; specializing a judge to a benchmark with in-context historic answers (the "Master of One" autorater recipe, arXiv:2411.15387) is a template worth adapting.
  • Name the threat model. "Survives gaming" means different things at eval time (style mimicry, contamination, benchmark-specific tuning) and at train time (RL directly against the metric). We test eval-time robustness first; train-time robustness is a separate, harder experiment.

Constraints and neighbors

  • Practical constraint, stated precisely: most frontier APIs return no (or only top-k) token log-probabilities, so teacher-forcing on frontier models is impractical today: expensive or noisy, not impossible in principle. Near-term work therefore runs on open weights or on output-based signals.
  • Neighbors we build on, not against: debate-based oversight (Aryan and Eric's paper, openreview.net/forum?id=MDArMFusA7) and reference-free mechanism design (TVD-MI) target the no-gold-reference regime; our boundary map says where the cheap with-reference signals stop working, which is exactly where those methods need to take over.
One map, two lanes: with references, make scoring judge-free and auditable; without references, know from the map that you have crossed into the regime where debate and mechanism design are the right tools.

Appendix · saturation mechanics

Why easy data kills the signal: the TFA range collapses 3x

~0.03TFA range across the ladder, GSM8K
~0.08TFA range, Putnam

On near-ceiling data the whole 5-model ladder is squeezed into a 0.03-wide TFA band; on hard data the band is three times wider. When the skill-driven spread shrinks below the size of a family style offset, style wins and rankings can invert. This is the mechanical link between the histogram's two lobes on the within-family slide.

Appendix · reconciliation

The original TFA paper's 0.66 is our Kendall τ on the full model set

Putnam-AXIOM reported TFA-vs-accuracy at 0.66 (MATH) and 0.52 (Putnam), well below our within-family values. There is no disagreement, only a metric and model-set difference, which the triplicate-statistics habit makes visible immediately: their 0.66 matches our Kendall τ on the full 17-model set including the math-specialized outliers (Qwen-Math, DeepSeek-Math, Mathstral, which reproduce gold style beyond their skill); dropping those outliers and reading Spearman recovers +0.86/+0.88.

Two papers, one dataset, no contradiction, and a live demonstration of why single-statistic reporting misleads.

The item-level conclusions do not depend on which judge we appointed

0.75-0.94inter-judge agreement (ρ)
2 judge familiesgpt-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8

The ranking results are judge-free (TFA vs accuracy). The item-level results are the only judge-defined ones, so we re-graded the three anchor datasets with a second frontier judge from a different model family under the same rubric: the MATH null stays null, the small GSM8K and Putnam signals replicate with confidence intervals excluding zero.

Appendix · the nuisance decomposition

The 89-96%, step by step, with a toy example

94.6%MATH-500
88.9%MATH-full
89.1%GSM8K
96.1%Putnam

The recipe (a one-way ANOVA on the reference)

  1. Build the grid. T[model, item] = per-item TFA for the 5-model Qwen ladder on the shared problems.
  2. Remove each model's level. Subtract each model's own mean: D = T minus its row mean. This strips overall generosity (the ranking axis), leaving item-to-item variation.
  3. Find the shared part. Average each item's column across models: b[item], the deviation identical for every model, a fact about the reference.
  4. Take the ratio. nuisance = Σb² / ΣD² = 89-96% on every dataset; the leftover 4-11% is the model-specific residual grading would need.

Reproducible via scripts/variance_decomp.py.

A two-model, three-item toy

item 1item 2item 3row mean
Model A0.700.800.900.80
Model B0.740.840.940.84

Center each row and both become [−.10, 0, +.10]: the item effect explains everything, nuisance = 100%. Item 3 is easier to reproduce for both models by the same amount, so nothing distinguishes them per-item; the uniform +0.04 on Model B is the ranking axis, removed in step 2.

Why one number gives both verdicts. Identical-across-models means it cancels in the average (ranking survives) and swamps any single item (grading dies).
Appendix · the other lane

The scalable-oversight program (no-gold-references), for discussion

Status: framing under discussion. This program targets the regime without gold references, the reverse of the deck's main lane, and is kept here as the long-horizon agenda. Two design stances updated after review: trained-offline metrics are admissible (they are hard to game outside RL loops), and every robustness claim must name its threat model, eval-time gaming vs train-time optimization against the metric.

1 · The yardstick

With little ground truth, split a judge's score into real quality signal vs surface nuisance from a small labeled anchor. Everything below needs this number.

2 · Survives smarter models

Does judge reliability fall predictably as the judged model outgrows the judge, and does the nuisance fraction predict the slope?

3 · Survives optimization

When a model is optimized against the judge (train-time threat model), which judges break, and is that predictable ex ante from the nuisance fraction?

4 · Design

What lowers the nuisance fraction: environment-grounded process signals, ensembles, consistency, debate, offline-trained specialized judges (arXiv:2411.15387)?

5 · The floor

Is there an open-ended regime where no cheap judge survives and the honest design keeps a human or an environment oracle in the loop?

The spine is one static quantity, the nuisance fraction, predicting both capability-gap collapse and hackability. Whether to pivot the group's effort to this lane is exactly the discussion to have.
